title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Grief, Loss & End-of-Life Care
html:
Loss, serious illness, and dying affect the whole person and the people important to them. The RN protects dignity, assesses comfort, listens without imposing personal beliefs, supports informed choices, and coordinates care with the interprofessional team. End-of-life nursing is active care: goals shift toward what matters most to the client, relief of suffering, and support for family or chosen support persons.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish palliative care, hospice care, and end-of-life care.
  • Respond therapeutically to grief without assuming a fixed sequence.
  • Verify advance-care wishes and current medical orders through the approved process.
  • Recognize common changes near death while assessing potentially treatable distress.
  • Provide individualized physical, emotional, cultural, and spiritual comfort.
  • Describe respectful care and required actions after death.

Use precise terms

Palliative care focuses on relief of symptoms, stress, and suffering during serious illness and can occur alongside disease-directed treatment. Hospice is a specific model for a person approaching the end of life whose plan emphasizes comfort rather than curative treatment, subject to eligibility and local requirements. End-of-life care describes support around the dying process. Do not tell a client that accepting palliative care means giving up.

Grief is individual

Grief can occur before or after a death and may follow many kinds of loss. Reactions can include sadness, anger, numbness, guilt, relief, anxiety, sleep or appetite changes, and difficulty concentrating. These responses do not unfold in a required order. Use presence, silence, open questions, reflection, and practical support. Avoid promises such as “everything happens for a reason” or comparisons with someone else's loss.

Assess safety directly
Grief does not automatically mean mental illness, but statements of hopelessness, self-harm, or inability to stay safe require direct assessment, immediate protection, and the appropriate response pathway.

Center the client's choices

When the client has decision-making capacity, the client directs care choices. Advance directives communicate preferences for future care when the person cannot speak for themself; laws and forms vary by jurisdiction. A health care proxy or surrogate does not replace the choices of a client who currently has capacity. Verify documents, current code-status orders, and the legally authorized decision-maker according to policy. If wishes, orders, and family requests conflict, continue comfort and safety, clarify promptly with the responsible clinician, and use ethics or other support resources as appropriate.

Goals and preferences can change. Ask what matters now, what symptoms are most troubling, whom the client wants involved, and whether cultural, spiritual, language, privacy, or ritual needs should shape care. Use a qualified interpreter when needed. Do not assume beliefs based on identity, and do not discuss the client as though they are absent.

Assess and relieve suffering

Comfort assessment remains systematic: pain; breathlessness; anxiety or agitation; nausea; constipation; mouth dryness; skin pressure or moisture; urinary or bowel needs; fatigue; sleep; temperature comfort; and emotional, social, or spiritual distress. Use the client's report whenever possible and behavioral cues when communication is limited. Administer ordered treatments, use appropriate nonpharmacologic measures, and reassess both relief and adverse effects.

Reduced appetite and fluid intake, increasing sleep, weakness, decreased urine output, cool or mottled extremities, altered breathing patterns, and changes in alertness may occur as death approaches. Explain expected changes in plain language while avoiding exact predictions. A new change still needs assessment: do not label every symptom “just dying” without considering the care plan, reversible causes, and the client's goals.

Support breathing and mouth comfort

For breathlessness, position for comfort, reduce unnecessary exertion, provide a calm presence, and administer ordered therapies. Oxygen may help when indicated but a saturation number alone does not define comfort. For dry mouth, provide frequent oral care and lip moisture with approved products. Do not force food or fluids; follow swallowing safety, goals, orders, and the plan developed with the client and team.

Include family and chosen support persons

With the client's permission, explain what to expect, invite questions, and offer specific ways to participate. Check understanding rather than overwhelming people with information. Family members may disagree or grieve differently. The RN maintains respect, protects the client's expressed preferences, and seeks help for conflict that threatens safe or goal-concordant care. Caregivers also need rest, resources, and bereavement support.

After death

Follow law and organizational policy for pronouncement or verification, required notifications, organ or tissue donation procedures, medical examiner or coroner involvement, and release of the body. Before postmortem care, determine whether lines or tubes must remain for examination or donation processes. Protect privacy and identification, handle belongings according to policy, and honor requested cultural or spiritual practices when possible. Document objective findings, notifications, valuables, and care provided. Give loved ones time and clear guidance; do not rush them because routine tasks are waiting.

Clinical example

A client receiving comfort-focused care becomes less responsive and develops irregular breathing. The daughter asks whether the client is suffering. The RN assesses facial expression, muscle tension, breathing effort, secretions, and other signs of distress; provides ordered comfort measures; explains that breathing patterns can change near death without promising an exact timeline; and asks what support the family needs. If distress persists, the RN promptly contacts the palliative or responsible team and reassesses the response.
